import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Palindromic primes

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Palindromic prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/palindromic_prime)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
-/

namespace PalindromicPrime

/--
Are there infinitely many palindromic primes in every base $b \geq 2$? Here a prime $p$ is
palindromic in base $b$ when its canonical digit list `Nat.digits b p`, with no leading zeros,
reads the same forwards and backwards. The bound on $b$ excludes the degenerate base-zero and
base-one definitions of `Nat.digits`.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem palindromic_prime :
    answer(sorry) ↔
      ∀ b : ℕ, 2 ≤ b → Set.Infinite {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ (Nat.digits b p).Palindrome} := by
  sorry

end PalindromicPrime
modeling_decisions: Interpreted “to every base” as: for each fixed natural-number base b ≥ 2, there are infinitely many primes palindromic in that base. The universal quantifier is inside a single `answer(sorry)` biconditional.
Restricted bases to b ≥ 2 because `Nat.digits` has special degenerate definitions at bases 0 and 1.
Represented the canonical base-b expansion by `Nat.digits b p`. It has no leading zeros for b ≥ 2; although its order is little-endian, list palindromicity is invariant under reversal.
Expressed palindromicity directly with Mathlib's `List.Palindrome` predicate on the digit list, and primality with `Nat.Prime`.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Palindromic primes

A *palindromic prime* is a prime number whose digit string, in a given base $b \ge 2$, reads the
same forwards and backwards. The first few decimal palindromic primes are
$2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 101, 131, 151, \ldots$ ([A002385](https://oeis.org/A002385)).
Banks, Hart and Sakata showed that, in every base, almost all palindromes are composite, but it is
not known whether there are infinitely many palindromic primes in any single base.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Palindromic prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/palindromic_prime)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [Banks, Hart, Sakata, *Almost all palindromes are composite*](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0405056)
-/

namespace PalindromicPrime

/--
Are there infinitely many palindromic primes to every base?

That is, is it true that for every base $b \ge 2$ there are infinitely many primes $p$ whose
base-$b$ digit string (without leading zeros, as given by `Nat.digits`) is a palindrome?

The restriction $b \ge 2$ excludes the degenerate "bases" $0$ and $1$, for which `Nat.digits`
does not give a positional numeral system.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem palindromic_prime :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ b : ℕ, 2 ≤ b → {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ (Nat.digits b p).Palindrome}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/--
The base-$10$ case: are there infinitely many decimal palindromic primes
([A002385](https://oeis.org/A002385))?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem palindromic_prime.variants.base_ten :
    answer(sorry) ↔ {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ (Nat.digits 10 p).Palindrome}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/-- Sanity check: $131$ is a decimal palindromic prime. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem palindromic_prime_131 : 131 ∈ {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ (Nat.digits 10 p).Palindrome} := by
  refine ⟨by norm_num, ?_⟩
  rw [List.Palindrome.iff_reverse_eq]
  norm_num

/-- Sanity check: $13$ is prime but is not a decimal palindrome. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem not_palindromic_prime_13 : 13 ∉ {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ (Nat.digits 10 p).Palindrome} := by
  simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq, not_and, List.Palindrome.iff_reverse_eq]
  intro _
  norm_num

/-- Sanity check: $7 = 111_2$ is a binary palindromic prime (a Mersenne prime). -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem palindromic_prime_binary_7 : 7 ∈ {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ (Nat.digits 2 p).Palindrome} := by
  refine ⟨by norm_num, ?_⟩
  rw [List.Palindrome.iff_reverse_eq]
  norm_num

end PalindromicPrime

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Palindromic primes

A *palindromic prime* (or *palprime*) is a prime number that is also a palindromic number,
i.e. its digits in some base $b$ read the same forwards and backwards. Palindromicity depends
on the base, while primality does not. The first decimal palindromic primes are
$2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 101, 131, 151, \dots$ and in binary they include the Mersenne and Fermat primes.

It is not known whether there are infinitely many palindromic primes in base $10$, or indeed in
any base. For every base, almost all palindromes are composite (Banks, Hart and Sakata).

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Palindromic prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/palindromic_prime)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [OEIS A002385](https://oeis.org/A002385) (decimal palindromic primes)
- [OEIS A117697](https://oeis.org/A117697) (binary palindromic primes)
- W. D. Banks, D. N. Hart, M. Sakata, *Almost all palindromes are composite*,
  Math. Res. Lett. 11 (2004), [arXiv:math/0405056](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0405056)
-/

namespace PalindromicPrime

/-- A natural number $n$ is a *base-$b$ palindrome* if its base-$b$ digit string (with no
leading zeros, as given by `Nat.digits`) reads the same forwards and backwards. -/
def IsBasePalindrome (b n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  (Nat.digits b n).Palindrome

instance (b n : ℕ) : Decidable (IsBasePalindrome b n) :=
  inferInstanceAs (Decidable (Nat.digits b n).Palindrome)

/-- `131` is a base-`10` palindrome. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem isBasePalindrome_ten_131 : IsBasePalindrome 10 131 := by
  decide +kernel

/-- `132` is not a base-`10` palindrome. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem not_isBasePalindrome_ten_132 : ¬ IsBasePalindrome 10 132 := by
  decide +kernel

/-- `5 = 101₂` is a base-`2` palindrome. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem isBasePalindrome_two_5 : IsBasePalindrome 2 5 := by
  decide +kernel

/-- `10 = 1010₂` is not a base-`2` palindrome. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem not_isBasePalindrome_two_10 : ¬ IsBasePalindrome 2 10 := by
  decide +kernel

/-- A base $b \ge 2$ is never a palindrome in base $b$, since it is written `10`. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem not_isBasePalindrome_self (b : ℕ) (hb : 2 ≤ b) : ¬ IsBasePalindrome b b := by
  have h : Nat.digits b b = [0, 1] := by
    rw [Nat.digits_def' (by omega) (by omega), Nat.mod_self, Nat.div_self (by omega),
      Nat.digits_of_lt b 1 one_ne_zero (by omega)]
  intro hpal
  rw [IsBasePalindrome, h, List.Palindrome.iff_reverse_eq] at hpal
  simp at hpal

/--
**Palindromic primes.** Are there infinitely many palindromic primes to every base?

That is, is it true that for every base $b \ge 2$ there are infinitely many primes whose
base-$b$ digit string is a palindrome? This is open for every base, including base $10$.

The bases are restricted to $b \ge 2$ because `Nat.digits` degenerates for $b = 0, 1$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem palindromic_prime :
    answer(sorry) ↔
      ∀ b : ℕ, 2 ≤ b → Set.Infinite {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ IsBasePalindrome b p} := by
  sorry

end PalindromicPrime
attempts.decomposition_objections: None. The single slot and its prescribed shape are the natural faithful reading of the list entry, and I followed them exactly.
modeling_decisions: Bases are restricted to `2 ≤ b`: for b = 0 and b = 1, `Nat.digits` gives `[n]` resp. `replicate n 1`, so every n would be a palindrome and the claim would be trivially true; the restriction is stated in the theorem docstring.

Palindromicity is defined via Mathlib's `List.Palindrome` applied to `Nat.digits b n` (little-endian digits, no leading zeros); `List.Palindrome` is symmetric under reversal so the endianness is irrelevant. `0` has digit list `[]` (a palindrome) but is not prime, so this does not affect the statement.

The quantifier over bases is placed inside the biconditional (`answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ b ≥ 2, ...`), giving one yes/no answer for all bases as the list-entry question asks, rather than one answer per base. The alternative parse 'primes palindromic in every base simultaneously' is excluded (and the test `not_isBasePalindrome_self` documents that b is never a base-b palindrome for b ≥ 2).
Test theorems use `decide +kernel` because `Nat.digits` is defined by well-founded recursion and plain `decide` does not reduce; `+kernel` avoids `native_decide`'s extra axiom.

The primary reference URL is written as https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/palindromic_prime as required; the module docstring also cites the Wikipedia unsolved-problems list, OEIS A002385/A117697 and Banks–Hart–Sakata (arXiv:math/0405056).

(without leading zeros), read the same forwards and backwards. For example, in base $10$
the palindromic primes begin $2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 101, 131, 151, 181, 191, 313, \dots$
(OEIS A002385), and in base $2$ they begin $11_2 = 3, 101_2 = 5, 111_2 = 7, 10001_2 = 17, \dots$
(OEIS A117697).

It is an open problem whether there are infinitely many palindromic primes to every base. This is
not known even for base $10$. Banks, Hart and Sakata showed that, in any base, almost all
palindromes are composite.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Palindromic prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/palindromic_prime)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [OEIS A002385](https://oeis.org/A002385)
- [OEIS A117697](https://oeis.org/A117697)
- W. D. Banks, D. N. Hart, M. Sakata, *Almost all palindromes are composite*,
  Math. Res. Lett. 11 (2004), 853–868. [arXiv:math/0405056](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0405056)
-/

namespace PalindromicPrime

/-- A natural number $n$ is a *base-$b$ palindrome* if its base-$b$ digits (without leading
zeros) read the same forwards and backwards. -/
def IsBasePalindrome (b n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  (Nat.digits b n).Palindrome

instance (b n : ℕ) : Decidable (IsBasePalindrome b n) :=
  inferInstanceAs (Decidable (Nat.digits b n).Palindrome)

/-- `131` is a base-`10` palindrome. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem isBasePalindrome_ten_131 : IsBasePalindrome 10 131 := by
  decide +kernel

/-- `130` is not a base-`10` palindrome. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem not_isBasePalindrome_ten_130 : ¬ IsBasePalindrome 10 130 := by
  decide +kernel

/-- `17 = 10001_2` is a base-`2` palindrome. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem isBasePalindrome_two_17 : IsBasePalindrome 2 17 := by
  decide +kernel

/-- `10 = 1010_2` is not a base-`2` palindrome. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem not_isBasePalindrome_two_10 : ¬ IsBasePalindrome 2 10 := by
  decide +kernel

/--
**Palindromic primes conjecture.** Are there infinitely many palindromic primes to every base?

That is, is it true that for every base $b \ge 2$ there are infinitely many primes $p$ whose
base-$b$ digits form a palindrome? The question is open for every base, including base $10$.

The restriction $b \ge 2$ excludes the degenerate "bases" $0$ and $1$, in which every natural
number is trivially a palindrome.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem palindromic_prime :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ b ≥ 2, {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ IsBasePalindrome b p}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/--
**Palindromic primes conjecture.** Are there infinitely many palindromic primes to every base?

That is, is it true that for every base $b \ge 2$ there are infinitely many primes $p$ whose
base-$b$ digits form a palindrome? The question is open for every base, including base $10$.

number is trivially a palindrome.
-/

theorem palindromic_prime :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ b ≥ 2, {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ IsBasePalindrome b p}.Infinite := by
  sorry

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Palindromic primes

A palindromic prime is a prime number that is also a palindromic number. Palindromicity
depends on the base of the number system, while primality does not. It is not known whether
there are infinitely many palindromic primes in base $10$, nor in any other base.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Palindromic prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/palindromic_prime)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [OEIS A002385](https://oeis.org/A002385), palindromic primes in base $10$
- [OEIS A117697](https://oeis.org/A117697), palindromic primes in base $2$
-/

namespace PalindromicPrime

/-- A natural number $n$ is a *base-$b$ palindrome* if its base-$b$ digit string (written
without leading zeros, as `Nat.digits` does) reads the same forwards and backwards. -/
def IsBasePalindrome (b n : ℕ) : Prop :=
  (Nat.digits b n).Palindrome

/-- `131` is a base-$10$ palindrome. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem isBasePalindrome_ten_131 : IsBasePalindrome 10 131 := by
  rw [IsBasePalindrome, List.Palindrome.iff_reverse_eq]
  norm_num

/-- `13` is not a base-$10$ palindrome. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem not_isBasePalindrome_ten_13 : ¬ IsBasePalindrome 10 13 := by
  rw [IsBasePalindrome, List.Palindrome.iff_reverse_eq]
  norm_num

/-- `5 = 101₂` is a base-$2$ palindrome. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem isBasePalindrome_two_5 : IsBasePalindrome 2 5 := by
  rw [IsBasePalindrome, List.Palindrome.iff_reverse_eq]
  norm_num

/-- `10 = 1010₂` is not a base-$2$ palindrome. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem not_isBasePalindrome_two_10 : ¬ IsBasePalindrome 2 10 := by
  rw [IsBasePalindrome, List.Palindrome.iff_reverse_eq]
  norm_num

/-- `2 = 10₂` is not a base-$2$ palindrome; the first binary palindromic prime is `3 = 11₂`. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem not_isBasePalindrome_two_2 : ¬ IsBasePalindrome 2 2 := by
  rw [IsBasePalindrome, List.Palindrome.iff_reverse_eq]
  norm_num

/-- `131` is a base-$10$ palindromic prime. -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem mem_palindromicPrimes_ten_131 : 131 ∈ {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ IsBasePalindrome 10 p} :=
  ⟨by norm_num, isBasePalindrome_ten_131⟩

/-- Are there infinitely many palindromic primes to every base?

That is, is it true that for every base $b \geq 2$ there are infinitely many primes $p$ whose
base-$b$ digit string is a palindrome? The bases are restricted to $b \geq 2$ because
positional notation degenerates for $b = 0$ and $b = 1$. -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem palindromic_prime :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ b ≥ 2, {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ IsBasePalindrome b p}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/-- Are there infinitely many palindromic primes in base $10$? -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem palindromic_prime.variants.base_ten :
    answer(sorry) ↔ {p : ℕ | p.Prime ∧ IsBasePalindrome 10 p}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end PalindromicPrime
attempts.decomposition_objections: None. The single-slot decomposition and its notes (b ≥ 2, ∀ inside the biconditional, Nat.digits-based palindromicity, rejection of the 'every base simultaneously' parse) are correct and were followed exactly.
modeling_decisions: Bases restricted to b ≥ 2 (`∀ b ≥ 2`), since `Nat.digits 0 n = [n]` and `Nat.digits 1 n = replicate n 1` make every number trivially palindromic; the docstring explains this restriction. (Without the restriction the statement would in fact be equivalent, since bases 0 and 1 make all primes palindromic, but the restriction is the faithful reading of 'base'.)

The universal quantifier over bases sits inside the biconditional, so `answer(True)` means 'yes, for every base there are infinitely many' and `answer(False)` means 'no, some base b ≥ 2 has only finitely many palindromic primes' — a single answer, as the list entry poses a single question. The alternative parse 'infinitely many primes palindromic in every base simultaneously' was rejected (no n ≥ 3 is palindromic in base n), per the decomposition notes.

Palindromicity is defined on `Nat.digits b n`, the little-endian digit list without leading zeros; a list is a palindrome iff its reverse is, so endianness does not affect the predicate. `List.Palindrome` from Mathlib is used rather than `l = l.reverse` for readability; tests are proved via `List.Palindrome.iff_reverse_eq` + `norm_num` because `Nat.digits` is defined by well-founded recursion and plain `decide` does not reduce it.
Primality is `Nat.Prime` (`p.Prime`), matching the sibling file FactorialPrime.lean; TwinPrimes.lean uses `Prime p` (the general `Prime`), which is equivalent on ℕ.
